The Constitutional Development of India: key facts from the book

Acts Passed for the British East India

Company Rule (1773-1853)

  • The Regulating Act of 1773 designated the governor of Bengal, Warren Hastings, as the Governor General of Bengal and subsumed the Presidencies of Madras and Bombay under Bengal's control.
  • The Governor General was provided with an executive council of four to assist him in Military and Non - Military decisions which would be made by the majority of the council.
  • Governor General could vote only in case of tie, in other words Governal-General had a casting vote in case of an equal division.
  • A Supreme Court which had a Chief Justice and three other Judges, was established at Fort William in Calcutta in the year 1774 by this Act. This Act prohibited the Servants of the company from engaging in private trade or accepting gifts and bribes from the Indians.
  • The British Government strengthened its control over the company through the Court of Directors (Governing body of The Company) to report on its revenue, civil and military affairs in India.
  • Pitts India Act 1784 distinguished between the commercial and political functions of the company.
  • Board of Control was created for political matters, and the Court of Directors controlled the commercial affairs.
  • Board of Control was comprised of 6 people.
  • Act of 1786 provided that Governor General could overrule his council in matters of importance affecting the safety, peace or interest of the Empire in India.
  • Governor General was granted the powers of Commander-in-Chief.
  • Lord Cornwallis was the first Governor General to enjoy these powers.
  • The Charter Act of 1793 further extended the commercial monopoly of the company for another 20 years.
  • Charter Act of 1813 for the first time, made provision of at least 1 Lakh rupees per year to be spent on the education, revival and improvement of literature, etc. of Indians. It ended the company's monopoly over trade, although the monopoly over trade of tea & trade with China continued.
  • Charter Act of 1833 made the Governor General of Bengal the Governor General of India and vested in him all civil and military powers.
  • Lord William Bentinck became the first Governor General of India.
  • It ended the Activities of East India Company as a commercial body, which became purely an administrative body.
  • A legal member (fourth member) was included in the council (executive) of Governor General.
  • Macaulay was the first legal member. This law member was entitled to act only for legislative purposes.
  • Charter Act of 1853 separated for the first time the legislative and executive functions of the Governor General's council.
  • It established a separate Indian (Central) legislative council for law-making.
  • It introduced an open competition system for the selection and recruitment of Civil Servants.
Acts Passed under the British Crown (1858-1947): key facts from the book
  • The British Crown decided to assume sovereignty over India from the East India Company by the Government of India Act 1858.
  • The Governor General also came to be called the 'Viceroy' of India. He became the direct representative of the British Crown.
  • Lord Canning became the first Viceroy of India.
  • The Board of Control and Court of Directors came to an end. A new post that was the Secretary of State of India was created.
  • He was assisted by a council of 15 members. He received the powers so long enjoyed by the Court of Directors and Board of Control.
  • The council of India was to be advisory in nature, in most cases the initiatives and the final decision remained with the Secretary of State for India. Indian Councils Act 1861, initiated the participation of the Indian representatives in law-making process.
  • The Act restored the legislative powers of making and amending laws to the provinces of Madras and Bombay, thus initiating the process of decentralization.
  • The Act empowered the Viceroy to issue ordinances in case of emergency, which were not to remain in force for more than six months. Indian Councils Act 1892, increased the number of non-official members in both the Central and Provincial Legislative councils but maintained the official majority in them.
  • The Indian members were granted the right to ask questions and discuss the budget in the legislative council.
  • This Act introduced the principle of election, in a limited sense, though the word 'election' was very carefully avoided in it. Indian Councils Act 1909 is also known as the Morley-Minto Reforms.
  • It provided (for the first time) for the association of Indians with the executive councils of Viceroy & Governors. Satyendra Prasad (Prasanna) Sinha became the first Indian to join the Viceroy's Executive Council. He was appointed as a law member.
  • The functions and size of legislatures both at the centre and in the provinces were enlarged. The members of council were given the right to discussion and ask Supplementary questions. The Act provided separate electorates for Muslims. Hence Lord Minto came to be known as The father of the communal electorate. Government of India Act 1919 is known by the name of ‘Montague-Chelmsford Reforms.
  • This Act, for the first time, adopted the Direct Election system.
  • Principle of communal representation was extended by providing separate electorates for Sikhs, Indian Christians, Europeans and Anglo - Indians. It introduced Bicameralism at Central level.
  • It separated various subjects, as the Central and provincial subjects. The Bicameral Central Legislature could make laws for the whole of British India.
  • It introduced dyarchy in the provinces.
  • Provincial subjects were further divided into two parts: transferred and reserved. For the first time, the term, responsible Government was used.
  • Under this Act, a commission was to be constituted after 10 years which will review the working of this Act and present its report. In November 1927 (i.e. 2 years before the schedule), the British Government announced the appointment of a seven- member statutory commission under the chairmanship of Simon to report on the condition of India under its new constitution. The commission was hence called the Simon Commission.
  • Government of India Act 1935 provided for the establishment of an All India Federation consisting of provinces and Princely states as units.
  • It provided for dyarchy at the centre (Which never came into existence) and abolished the same in the provinces.
  • It provided for the establishment of a Reserve Bank of India to control the currency and credit of the country.
  • Principle of Communal representation was further extended by providing separate electorates for Scheduled Castes, women and labourers.
  • A Federal Court was set up in 1937 through this Act.
  • This Act separated Burma from the British India and established two new provinces-Sindh and Orissa (now Odisha).
  • It introduced bicameralism in 6 out of 11 provinces. Indian Independence Act of1947 declared India to be an Independent dominion nation on 15 August 1947.
  • It abolished the office of Viceroy and, a Governor General was appointed for each dominion.
  • It dropped the title of 'Emperor of India' from the royal titles of the King of the United Kingdom.
  • In which of the following Acts, the provision was made for the establishment of Supreme Court at Calcutta?Regulating Act, 1773

Regulating Act 1773 → Supreme Court at Fort William, Calcutta; set up in 1774; first Chief Justice Sir Elijah Impey. Must know

    Constituent Assembly and making of the Constitution

    48 facts · 72 questions · 11 Must know

    Read the key facts and each question with its answer (30 min), then cover the answers and recall (10 min). Open the chapter in the full notes for explanations.
    Constituent Assembly and making of the Constitution: key facts from the book
    • The first formal demand for the Constituent Assembly was made by the Swaraj Party at a conference in Ranchi held in May, 1934.
    • The idea of a Constituent Assembly was put forward for the first time by M.N. Roy in the year 1934.
    • The Indian National Congress officially demanded (after the Swaraj Party) a Constituent Assembly to frame the Constitution of India for the first time in May 1934, at Patna.
    • In 1938, Jawahar Lal Nehru, on behalf of the INC, declared that the constitution of free India must be framed, without outside interference, by a constituent Assembly elected on the basis of adult Franchise. The Demand was finally accepted in principle in the August offer of 1940.
    • The Constituent Assembly was constituted under the scheme formulated by the Cabinet Mission Plan 1946.
    • Number of representatives from provinces was based on their population i.e. about One representative per 10 Lakh people. Ofthese, 296 were to be allotted to British India and 93 Seats to the Princely States. Out of296 seats allotted to British India, 292 members were to be drawn from the eleven governor's provinces and four from the four Chief Commissioners' provinces, one from each.
    • The representatives of Princely states were to be nominated by the heads of the Princely states.
    • The elections to the constituent assembly for 296 seats were held in July-August 1946. The Indian National Congress won 208 seats, the Muslim League won 73 seats, and the small groups and independents got the remaining 15 seats.
    • In the beginning, Princely states did not participate in the Constituent Assembly, but with the third session of the Constituent Assembly commencing on 28 April, 1947 the representatives of the Princely States of India began to join it gradually.
    • Constituent Assembly was a result of an Indirect election.
    • This election was not based on the Adult franchise.
    • According to Government of India Act 1935, voting rights were limited and based on tax, education and property.
    • The Viceroy invited the elected representatives for the first meeting of Constituent Assembly on 9 December 1946.
    • 207 members participated in the first meeting. The meeting was presided over by Dr. Sachchidanand Sinha, the temporary President. Later, on 11 December 1946, Dr. Rajendra Prasad was unanimously elected as the President of the Constituent Assembly. It took 2 years, 11 months and 17 days (according to the Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha website) to complete the task of Constitution making.
    • A Total of 11 Sessions (165 days) were held.
    • On 26 November 1949, i.e. the last day of 11th session, the Constitution was adopted. Except for these 11 sessions the constituent assembly finally met on 24 January 1950 to get the signatures of the members on the constitution.
    • Benegal Narsing Rau (B.N. Rau) was appointed as the constitutional advisor to the assembly.
    • On 26 November 1949, the people of India adopted, enacted and gave to themselves the constitution of India.
    • Some provisions of the constitution came into force on 26 November 1949 itself but it completely came into force on 26 January 1950.
    • The number of women in the constituent assembly was 15.
    • They were 1- Vijayalakshmi Pandit, 2- Rajkumari Amrit Kaur, 3- Sarojini Naidu, 4- Sucheta Kripalani, 5- Purnima Bannerjee, 6- Leela Roy, 7- G. Durgabai, 8- Hansa Mehta, 9- Kamala Choudhry, 10- Renuka Ray, 11- Malati Choudhury, 12- Dakshayani Velayudhan, 13- Begum Aizaz Rasul, 14- Annie Mascarene and 15- Ammu Swaminathan.
    • The Interim government of India was formed on 2 September, 1946; however, it did not include any member from the Muslim League.
    • Finally on 26 October 1946, 5 Members of the Muslim League were also included in the Cabinet. Interim Cabinet- 1946

    • Who gave the idea of a Constituent Assembly firstly for the formation of Constitution for India?Swaraj party in 1934

    First Indian demand for a Constituent Assembly → Swaraj Party, Ranchi conference, May 1934; members to be elected on adult suffrage.

    Full question and explanation · 1 paper(s)

    • Who in the begining, presented the idea of Indian Constituent Assembly in pre independence days?M.N. Roy

    Idea of a Constituent Assembly first given by M.N. Roy in 1934; first formal demand by Swaraj Party, Ranchi, May 1934.

    Don't confuse The person who gave the idea (M.N. Roy) with the party that formally demanded it (Swaraj Party).

    Full question and explanation · 1 paper(s)

    • Who said, "The constituent Assembly alone can produce a Constitution indigenous to the country and truly and fully representing the will of the people"?Mahatma Gandhi

    Gandhi, 'The Only Way', Harijan, 19 November 1939: only a Constituent Assembly can produce an indigenous Constitution truly representing the people's will.

    Full question and explanation · 1 paper(s)

    • The proposal for framing of the Constitution of India by an elected Constituent Assembly was made byCripps Mission

    Proposal to frame India's Constitution by an elected Constituent Assembly (after Second World War) → Cripps Mission, 1942.

    Full question and explanation · 1 paper(s)

    • With reference to the proposals of Cripps Mission, consider the following statements:2 only

    Cripps Mission (March 1942): provincial members elected (not nominated) by provincial assemblies, princes nominate; a province rejecting the Constitution could sign separate agreement with Britain.

    Full question and explanation · 1 paper(s)

    • As per Cabinet Mission plan, in the Constituent Assembly to decide allotted members seat in each province, one representative was in ratio to which population?10 Lakh

    Cabinet Mission 1946 → Constituent Assembly seats by population: roughly one representative per 10 lakh people.

    Full question and explanation · 1 paper(s)

    • Who among the following persons was not a member of the Cabinet Mission?William Wood

    Cabinet Mission: Pethick-Lawrence (Secretary for India), Stafford Cripps (Board of Trade), A.V. Alexander (Navy); William Wood was not a member.

    Memory aid P-C-A: Pethick, Cripps, Alexander.

    Full question and explanation · 1 paper(s)

    • Indian Constituent Assembly was established under –Cabinet Mission, 1946

    Constituent Assembly was set up under the Cabinet Mission Plan, 1946, by indirect election. Must know

    Full question and explanation · 3 paper(s)

    • In the Interim Government formed in 1946, the Vice President of the Executive Council was.Jawaharlal Nehru

    Interim Government 1946: Viceroy was ex-officio President of Executive Council; Jawaharlal Nehru was Vice-President; announced 24 August, in charge by 2 September 1946.

    Full question and explanation · 1 paper(s)

    • Who of the following was not the member of the Interim National Government formed in August 1946 A.D.?Dr. S. Radhakrishnan

    Interim Government (announced 24 August 1946): Rajagopalachari – Education, Rajendra Prasad – Food and Agriculture, Jagjivan Ram – Labour; S. Radhakrishnan not a member. Must know

    Full question and explanation · 3 paper(s)

    • Assertion (A): According to the Wavell Plan, the number of Hindu and Muslim members in the Executive Council was to be equal.(A) is true, but (R) is false.

    Wavell Plan (June 1945) → equal Hindu and Muslim members in the Executive Council (true); the claim that Wavell saw this as avoiding partition is false.

    Full question and explanation · 1 paper(s)

    • Which of the following statement(s) is/are true in relation to Constituent Assembly?3 and 4

    Constituent Assembly: indirectly elected by provincial legislative assemblies (not adult suffrage, not direct); multi-party body; worked through many committees.

    Full question and explanation · 1 paper(s)

    • Which of the following statements are correct regarding to Indian Constituent Assembly? (A) It was not based on Adult Franchise. (B) It resulted from direct election. (C) It was not a multi-party body. (D) It worked through several committees. Select the correct answer using code given below: Code:(A) and (D)

    Constituent Assembly: not based on adult franchise; indirectly elected; multi-party (Congress, Muslim League, independents); worked through several committees.

          • The Drafting Committee was comprised of 7 members, including the chairman Dr. Bhim Rao Ambedkar. The other 6 members are as follows:

          Sources of the Constitution: key facts from the book
          • A major portion of the Indian Constitution is borrowed from the Government of India Act 1935 (Blue Print of Indian Constitution).
          • Rule of law, Parliamentary form of government, Cabinet System, Single Citizenship, Bicameral Legislature, Law making procedures, Parliamentary Privileges and prerogative writs are provisions borrowed from the Constitution of Britain.
          • Preamble, Judicial review, Independence of Judiciary, Fundamental rights, the post of Vice-President, the procedure of impeachment of President and removal of Supreme Court and High Courtjudges are provisions taken from the Constitution of the USA.
          • DPSP (Directive Principle of State Policy), method of election of President and nomination of members to the Council of States (Rajya Sabha) are provisions inspired by the Constitution of Ireland.
          • Federation with a strong centre, Advisory jurisdiction of the Supreme Court, residuary powers to be vested in the centre and appointment of Governors by the centre are provisions borrowed from Constitution of Canada.
          • Joint sitting of both houses of the Parliament, language of Preamble, Freedom of trade, commerce and intercourse and idea of concurrent list are borrowed from Constitution of Australia.
          • Provision related to Emergency (except Financial emergency) imported from Constitution of Germany. Procedure Established by law from Japan, procedure of the Constitutional Amendment and election of members of Rajya Sabha are borrowed from South Africa.
          • Fundamental Duties and the ideals of Justice (social, economic and political) in the preamble are imported from the USSR. The Republican system, principle of liberty, equality and fraternity in the preamble are borrowed from the Constitution of France.

                Parts of the Indian Constitution: key facts from the book
                • The Indian Constitution is divided into 22 parts. (at present, a total of 25 parts)
                • Part IV-A and Part XIV-A were added by the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976.
                • Part IX-A was added by the 74th Amendment Act, 1992.
                • Part IX-B was added by the 97th Amendment Act, 2011.

                Articles of the Constitution: key facts from the book
                • There were 22 parts, 395 Articles and 8 schedules in the original copy of the Constitution.
                • A number of Articles were added and removed later through amendments.
                • At present, there are around 468 articles, but these are added in the form of Articles inserted with alphanumeric suffixes such as 21A, 43B, etc. of the original Articles (395).

                Important articles of the Constitution at a glance :-

                1 -Name and territory of the Union.
                2 -Admission or establishment of new States.
                3 -Formation of new States and alteration of areas,

                boundaries or names of existing States.

                5 -Citizenship at the commencement of the Constitution.
                14 -Equality before law
                15 -Prohibition of discrimination on the grounds of religion,

                race, caste, sex or place of birth.

                16 -Equality of opportunity in matters of public employment.
                17 -Abolition of Untouchability.
                18 -Abolition of titles.
                19 -Protection of certain rights regarding freedom of speech,

                etc.

                20 -Protection in respect of conviction for offences.
                21 -Protection of life and personal liberty.

                21A - Right to education.

                22 -Protection against arrest and detention in certain cases.
                23 -Prohibition of traffic in human beings and forced

                labour.

                24 -Prohibition of employment of children in factories, etc.
                25 -Freedom of conscience and free profession, practice

                and propagation of religion.

                26 -Freedom to manage religious affairs.
                27 -Freedom as to payment of taxes for the promotion of

                any particular religion.

                28 - Freedom as to attendance at religious instruction or religious worship in certain educational institutions.

                29 -Protection of the interests of minorities.
                30 -Right of minorities to establish and administer

                educational institutions.

                32 - Remedies for enforcement of fundamental rights including writs.

                38 - State to secure a social order for the promotion of the welfare of the people.

                39 - Certain principles of policy to be followed by the State.

                39A - Equal justice and free legal aid.

                40 -Organisation of Village Panchayats.
                41 -Right to work, to education and to public assistance in

                certain cases.

                43 -Living wage, etc. for workers.
                44 -Uniform Civil Code for the citizens.
                45 -Provision for early childhood care and free &

                compulsory education to children below the age of six years.

                48 - Organisation of Agriculture and Animal Husbandry.

                48A - Protection and improvement of environment and safeguarding of forests and wild life.

                49 - Protection of monuments and places and objects of national importance.

                50 -Separation of judiciary from executive.
                51 -Promotion of international peace and security.

                51A - Fundamental Duties.

                52 -The President of India.
                53 -Executive power of the Union.
                54 -Election of President
                55 -Manner of Election of President.
                57 -Eligibility for re-election.
                58 -Qualifications for election as the President.
                60 -Oath or Affirmation by the President.
                61 -Procedure for impeachment of the President.
                63 -The Vice-President of India.
                64 -The Vice-President to be ex-officio Chairman of the

                Council of States.

                72 -Power of President to grant pardons, etc., and to

                suspend, remit or commute sentences in certain cases.

                      Schedules

                      54 facts · 64 questions · 12 Must know

                      Read the key facts and each question with its answer (30 min), then cover the answers and recall (10 min). Open the chapter in the full notes for explanations.
                      Schedules: key facts from the book
                      • The Constitution of India at the time of its adoption had only 8 schedules but, there are 12 schedules in our Constitution at present.
                      • First Schedule – States and Union Territories with territorial demarcation.
                      • Second Schedule – Provisions relating to the salary, emoluments and allowances of the various office bearers of the Union of India.
                      • Third Schedule – Forms of oaths and affirmations of the various office bearers of the Union of India.
                      • Fourth Schedule – Allocation of seats in the Council of States to the States and Union Territories.
                      • Fifth Schedule – Provisions relating to the administration and control of Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes.
                      • Sixth schedule – Provisions relating to the administration of tribal areas in the States of Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram.
                      • Seventh Schedule – Division of powers between the Union and the States. It contains three lists-

                      (i) Union List – Originally 97 subjects (presently 98) and only the centre has the power to make laws on these subjects.

                      (ii) State list – Originally 66 subjects (presently 59) and Primarily the States have the power to make laws on these subjects.

                      (iii) Concurrent list – Originally 47 subjects(presently 52) and on these subjects the centre and the States both have the power to make laws.

                      • Radio and Television, stock exchanges and future market, share market, Post Office, Banking, Census, Insurance, Defence, Railways and corporation taxes, etc. come under the Union list.
                      • Police, Public health and sanitation, gas, agriculture, railway police, prisons, Panchayati Raj or local Government and land reforms etc., come under the State list.
                      • Economic and Social planning, Criminal procedure, population control and family planning, education, Forests, Marriage, Divorce and adoptions etc., come in the Concurrent List.
                      • Eighth Schedule – Languages recognised by the Constitution. Originally, it had 14 languages, but presently, there are 22 languages.
                      • Sindhi was added by the 21st Constitutional Amendment Act of 1967.
                      • Konkani, Nepali and Manipuri were added by the 71st Amendment Act, 1992 and Bodo, Dogri, Maithili and Santhali were added by the 92nd Amendment Act, 2003. Oriya was renamed as Odia by the 96th Amendment Act, 2011.
                      • Ninth Schedule – Validation of certain Acts and Regulations (originally 13 but presently 284).
                      • It was added by the 1st Constitutional Amendment Act, 1951.
                      • Tenth Schedule – Provision relating to disqualification of the members of Parliament and State Legislatures on the ground of defection.
                      • It was added by the 52nd Amendment Act 1985. Also known as the Anti–Defection Law.
                      • Eleventh Schedule – Specifies the power, authority and responsibilities of Panchayats. It has 29 subjects. It was added by the 73rd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1992.
                      • Twelfth Schedule – Specifies the power, authority and responsibilities of Municipalities, etc. It has 18 subjects. It was added by the 74th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1992.
                      • Total number of Schedules in the Constitution is –12

                      12 Schedules now; originally 8; 9th added by 1st Amendment 1951 (validation of Acts); 10th by 52nd Amendment 1985 (anti-defection).

                      • The right of the government to impose taxes and fees is provided in which Schedule of Constitution?VII Schedule

                      Power to levy taxes and fees → Seventh Schedule (three lists); Art. 246 distributes legislative powers, including taxation, between Parliament and States.

                      Full question and explanation · 1 paper(s)

                      • Which one of the following statements is correct as per the Constitution of India?Inter-State quarantine is a Union subject under the Union List.

                      Inter-State quarantine and inter-State migration → Union List, Entry 81; inter-State trade and commerce → Union List, Entry 42; corporation tax is not a State subject.

                      Full question and explanation · 1 paper(s)

                      • Land Reform comes under the subjects of –State List

                      Land reforms → State List; land reform Acts protected by the Ninth Schedule, added by 1st Amendment Act, 1951.

                      Full question and explanation · 1 paper(s)

                      • Which one of the following Schedules of the Constitution of India contains provisions regarding Anti-defection law?Tenth Schedule

                      Anti-defection law → Tenth Schedule, added by 52nd Amendment Act, 1985; lays down disqualification of legislators on grounds of defection. Must know

                      Full question and explanation · 4 paper(s)

                      • Under which Schedule of the Constitution of India can the transfer of tribal land to private parties for mining be declared null and void?Fifth Schedule

                      Fifth Schedule (Scheduled Areas and Tribes) → Samatha vs State of Andhra Pradesh, 1997: transfer of tribal land to private parties for mining is void.

                      Full question and explanation · 1 paper(s)

                      • Ifa particular area is brought under the Fifth Schedule of the Constitution of India, which one of the following statements best reflects the consequence of it?This would prevent the transfer of land of tribal people to non-tribal people.

                      Area under Fifth Schedule → transfer of tribal land to non-tribals can be prevented; President declares scheduled areas (10 States have them); Governor can amend regulations.

                      Full question and explanation · 1 paper(s)

                      • The Fifth Schedule deals with the governance and protection of the interests of which specific group of people?Scheduled Tribes

                      Fifth Schedule → administration and control of Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes in all States except Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram.

                      Full question and explanation · 1 paper(s)

                      • Which Schedule of the Constitution of India contains special provisions for the administration and control of Scheduled Areas in several states?Fifth

                      Fifth Schedule → Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes, except in Assam, Tripura, Meghalaya, Mizoram, whose tribal areas fall under the Sixth Schedule.

                      Don't confuse Fifth (Scheduled Areas, several States) with Sixth (tribal areas of four North-East States).

                      Full question and explanation · 1 paper(s)

                      • The provisions of the fifth and Sixth Schedule in the Constitution of India are made to –Protect the interests of Scheduled Tribes

                      Fifth and Sixth Schedules → special provisions to protect the interests of Scheduled Tribes.

                      Full question and explanation · 1 paper(s)

                      • The 6th schedule of the Indian Constitution is related to the administration of Tribal areas of:Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura & Mizoram

                      Sixth Schedule → tribal areas of Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, Mizoram (through Arts 244(2), 275(1)); aim: preserve tribal culture.

                      Memory aid AMTM: Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, Mizoram.

                      Full question and explanation · 1 paper(s)

                      • Provisions of Schedule sixth of the Constitution does not apply to which of these state?Manipur

                      Sixth Schedule covers Assam, Tripura, Meghalaya and Mizoram; Manipur is not covered. Must know

                      Don't confuse Manipur is a North-East State but not a Sixth Schedule State.

                      Full question and explanation · 3 paper(s)

                      • Consider the following statements with reference to Scheduled areas:Both 1 and 2

                      Scheduled Areas → notified by President's order (Art. 244(1)); States with them must set up a Tribal Advisory Council (para 4, Fifth Schedule).

                      Full question and explanation · 1 paper(s)

                      • With reference to ‘Scheduled Areas’ in India, consider the following statements:Only two

                      Scheduled Area is notified by President's order (true); largest unit is the district, lowest a cluster of villages in a block (true); the Chief Ministers statement is false.

                      Full question and explanation · 1 paper(s)

                      • Consider the following statements: With reference to the Constitution of India, if an area in a State is declared as Scheduled Area under the Fifth Schedule I. the State Government loses its executive power in such areas and a local body assumes total administration. II. the Union Government can take over the total administration of such areas under certain circumstances on the recommendations of the Governor Which of the statements given above is/are correct?Neither I nor II

                      Fifth Schedule area: State keeps its executive power there (no local body takeover); Union cannot take over its administration on Governor's recommendation; both statements false.

                      Full question and explanation · 1 paper(s)

                      • What is/are true in relation to Autonomous Districts?(i) and (iii)

                      Sixth Schedule Autonomous District Council: 30 members (true); Governor directs how Parliament's Acts apply in Assam's autonomous districts (true); '24 elected, 6 nominated' is false.

                      Full question and explanation · 1 paper(s)

                      • The Eleventh Schedule of the Constitution is related to which of the following?Panchayati Raj

                      Eleventh Schedule → Panchayati Raj; added by 73rd Amendment, 1992; 29 subjects. Must know

                      Memory aid Panchayat trio: 73rd Amendment, Eleventh Schedule, 29 subjects.

                      Full question and explanation · 2 paper(s)

                      • The list of powers, authority and responsibilities which may be entrusted to the Panchayats is given in the:Eleventh Schedule

                      Powers and responsibilities of Panchayats → Eleventh Schedule (Art. 243G), added by 73rd Amendment Act 1992; 29 entries. Must know

                      Full question and explanation · 2 paper(s)

                            The Preamble

                            35 facts · 50 questions · 10 Must know

                            Read the key facts and each question with its answer (30 min), then cover the answers and recall (10 min). Open the chapter in the full notes for explanations.
                            The Preamble: key facts from the book
                            • The Objectives Resolution was moved to the Constituent Assembly on 13th December 1946 by Pt. Jawahar Lal Nehru, and it was adopted by the Constituent Assembly on 22 January 1947. Later, this Resolution became the foundation of the Preamble.
                            • The words ‘Socialist’, ‘Secular’, and ‘Integrity’ were incorporated in the Preamble by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act 1976.
                            • The Preamble declares India as a Sovereign, Socialist, Secular, Democratic Republic. It secures for all its citizens, justice of three types – social, economic and political. It is very helpful in the legal interpretation of the Indian Constitution.
                            • In the words of Sir Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar, “The Preamble to our Constitution expresses what we had thought or dreamt so long”.
                            • The Supreme Court accepted it as a part of the Constitution in the Keshavanand Bharti case(1973).
                            • Before this, in the Berubari case (1960), the Preamble was not considered a part of the Constitution.
                            • In Golaknath vs State of Punjab (1967), the preamble was considered as the core soul of the Constitution.
                            • In Bommai vs Union of India (1994), the Supreme Court again gave the concept that the Preamble is a part of the Constitution.
                            • It is non – justiciable in nature.
                            • It talks about the freedom of faith, belief, worship, expression and thought.
                            • It also ensures dignity and equal status and opportunities for all.
                            • It is called the soul of the Constitution.
                            • Dr. B. R. Ambedkar called the right to Constitutional remedies (Art. 32) as the heart and soul of the Constitution.
                            • K. M. Munshi called the Preamble the political horoscope.
                            • Subhash Kashyap said that, if the Constitution is the body then the preamble is the soul; if the Constitution is the building then the preamble is the foundation stone.
                            • Dr. B.R. Ambedkar said that “the Constitution is a pious paper.”
                            • In the following quotation, “WE THE PEOPLE OF INDIA, having solemnly resolved to constitute India into a Sovereign, Socialist, Secular, Democratic, Republic and to secure to all its citizens: JUSTICE, social, economic and political; LIBERTY of thought, expression, belief, faith, and worship; Equality of status and of opportunity: and to promote among them all; FRATERNITY assuring the dignity of the Individual and the unity and integrity of the Nation. In our Constituent Assembly, this ‘X’ do hereby adopt, enact and give to ourselves this Constitution.”, ‘X’ stands for:Twenty-sixth day of November, 1949

                            Preamble gives the adoption date → 'this twenty-sixth day of November, 1949'.

                            Full question and explanation · 1 paper(s)

                            • What was the exact Constitutional Status of the Indian Republic on 26-1-1950 when the Constitution came into force?A Sovereign Democratic Republic

                            On 26 January 1950 India was 'A Sovereign Democratic Republic'; 'socialist', 'secular' and 'integrity' were added by 42nd Amendment Act, 1976. Must know

                            Full question and explanation · 3 paper(s)

                            • The mind of the makers of the constitution of India is reflected in which of the following?The Preamble

                            Preamble reflects the mind of the Constitution's makers; K.M. Munshi called it the political horoscope.

                            Full question and explanation · 2 paper(s)

                            • How many types of justice, liberty, equality and fraternity in that order have been mentioned in the preamble of constitution of India?3, 5, 2, 1

                            Preamble: 3 types of justice, 5 of liberty, 2 of equality, 1 fraternity → 3, 5, 2, 1.

                            Memory aid Justice: social, economic, political (3); Liberty: thought, expression, belief, faith, worship (5); Equality: status, opportunity (2).

                            Full question and explanation · 1 paper(s)

                            • In the context of the Preamble of Indian Constitution which of the following sequence is correct?Sovereign, Socialist, Secular, Democratic, Republic

                            Preamble order: Sovereign, Socialist, Secular, Democratic, Republic (as amended by 42nd Amendment, 1976); word 'People's' is not in it (it is in China's Constitution).

                            Memory aid Three S's, then D, then R: SSS-D-R.

                            Full question and explanation · 1 paper(s)

                            • Which among the following words were inserted in the Preamble of the Indian Constitution by the 42nd Constitution Amendment?1 and 2

                            42nd Amendment inserted 'Socialist' and 'Secular' into the Preamble; 'Sovereign' and 'Republic' were already in the original Preamble.

                            Full question and explanation · 1 paper(s)

                            • Which among the following is the correct order mentioned in Preamble of the Indian Constitution?Sovereign, Socialist, Secular, Democratic

                            Preamble order: Sovereign → Socialist → Secular → Democratic → Republic; then Justice, Liberty, Equality, Fraternity. Must know

                            Full question and explanation · 3 paper(s)

                            • The expression "Socialist" was introduced in the Preamble of Indian Constitution by which amendment?42nd amendment

                            'Socialist' → added to the Preamble by 42nd Amendment Act (1976), along with 'secular' and 'integrity'. Must know

                            Full question and explanation · 4 paper(s)

                            • Which two words have been incorporated in the Preamble by 42nd Amendment?Secular and socialist

                            42nd Amendment Act 1976 (on Swaran Singh Committee's advice) → added 'Socialist', 'Secular' and 'Integrity' to the Preamble.

                            Full question and explanation · 1 paper(s)

                            • Which one of the following describes India as a Secular State?Preamble to the Constitution

                            Preamble describes India as a Secular State; 'Secular' was added by 42nd Amendment Act, 1976.

                            Full question and explanation · 1 paper(s)

                            • Which one of the following words was not included in the Preamble of the Indian Constitution in 1975?Integrity

                            'Integrity' was not in the Preamble in 1975; added in 1976 by 42nd Amendment; Fraternity, Sovereign, Equality were original words. Must know

                            Full question and explanation · 2 paper(s)

                            • Consider the following statements in regards to the Preamble of Constitution and select the correct one using the code given below -Only 1,2 and 4

                            Preamble: grew from Nehru's Objectives Resolution; non-justiciable; can be amended (Kesavananda Bharati, 1973); cannot override specific provisions of the Constitution. Must know

                            Full question and explanation · 2 paper(s)

                            • The Preamble of the Constitution was amended by-42nd Amendment

                            42nd Amendment, 1976 changed the Preamble: 'Sovereign Democratic Republic' → 'Sovereign Socialist Secular Democratic Republic'; 'unity of the Nation' → 'unity and integrity of the Nation'.

                            Full question and explanation · 1 paper(s)

                            • Which of the following words were not present in the preamble of the Indian Constitution adopted on November 26, 1949?(2), (3), (4)

                            Original Preamble (26 November 1949): Sovereign, Democratic, Republic. 'Socialist', 'Secular' and 'Integrity' added by 42nd Amendment, 1976; 'Reliable', 'Non-religious' never in it. Must know

                            Full question and explanation · 9 paper(s)

                            • The goal of Constitution is to secure/assure all its citizensAll above

                            Preamble secures: Justice (social, economic, political); Liberty (thought, expression, belief, faith, worship); Equality (status, opportunity); Fraternity (dignity of individual, unity and integrity).

                            Full question and explanation · 1 paper(s)

                            • Given below are two statements, one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other as Reason (R):Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).

                            'Sovereign socialist secular democratic republic' was substituted for 'Sovereign Democratic Republic' by 42nd Amendment Act 1976, the only Preamble amendment so far; A and R true.

                            Full question and explanation · 1 paper(s)

                            • India has people’s sovereignty because the Preamble of the Constitution begins with the words:We, the People of India

                            'We, the People of India' (opening words of the Preamble) → people's sovereignty: India is governed by its Constitution, not by any external power.

                            Full question and explanation · 2 paper(s)

                            • “All individuals are fully and equally human” this principle is known as –Universalism

                            'All individuals are fully and equally human' → Universalism: everyone is entitled to human rights without discrimination.

                            Full question and explanation · 1 paper(s)

                            • Which among the following is the correct expression of the term ‘Secular’ in India?There is no religion of the State in India.

                            Secular in India → no official religion of the State; State treats all religions equally (positive secularism).

                            Full question and explanation · 1 paper(s)

                            • Which of the following words is NOT mentioned in the Preamble of the Constitution of India?Federal

                            'Federal' is not in the Preamble; it has Sovereign, Socialist, Secular, Democratic, Republic.

                            Full question and explanation · 1 paper(s)

                            • Which of the following words is not in the Preamble to the Constitution of India?Public Welfare

                            'Public Welfare' is not in the Preamble; Socialist, Secular and Sovereign are.

                            Full question and explanation · 1 paper(s)

                            • Which one of the following liberty is not embodied in the Preamble of the Constitution of India?Economic Liberty

                            Preamble liberty → thought, expression, belief, faith and worship; economic liberty is not included. Must know

                            Full question and explanation · 2 paper(s)

                            • Which among the following is not mentioned in the Preamble to the Constitution of India?Religious Justice

                            Preamble justice → social, economic, political; 'religious justice' is not mentioned.

                            Full question and explanation · 1 paper(s)

                            • Which of the following is true in relation to the Preamble of Constitution of India?The words ‘Socialist’ and ‘Secular’ were not the part of the Preamble on the enforcement of Constitution in 1950

                            'Socialist' and 'Secular' were not in the Preamble when the Constitution came into force in 1950; inserted by 42nd Amendment Act, 1976 (not 1977 or 1985).

                            Full question and explanation · 1 paper(s)

                            • Which part of the Indian Constitution has been described as the ‘Soul’ of the Constitution?The Preamble

                            Preamble → 'Soul of the Constitution'; K.M. Munshi called it the 'horoscope of our sovereign democratic republic'. Must know

                            Full question and explanation · 5 paper(s)

                            • Who has termed Constitution a sacred document?B. R. Ambedkar

                            B.R. Ambedkar → held that the Constitution must be treated as a basic and sacred document; chaired the Drafting Committee from 1947.

                            Full question and explanation · 1 paper(s)

                            • In which case did the Supreme Court first declare that the Preamble is not a part of the Constitution?Berubari

                            Berubari case (1960) → Supreme Court first held that the Preamble is not an integral part of the Constitution.

                            Full question and explanation · 1 paper(s)

                            • In which of the following cases Supreme Court held that ‘The Preamble forms part of the Constitution?Bommai Vs. Union of India

                            S.R. Bommai vs Union of India (1994) → Preamble is an integral part of the Constitution; Kesavananda Bharati (1973, 13 judges) → Basic Structure doctrine.

                            Full question and explanation · 1 paper(s)

                            • In which of the following cases the Supreme Court regarded Preamble as a part of the basic structure of India Constitution?Keshwanand Bharti Case

                            Kesavananda Bharati case → Supreme Court treated the Preamble as part of the basic structure of the Constitution.

                            Full question and explanation · 1 paper(s)

                            • The ideals and objectives outlined in the Preamble of the Indian Constitution have been further elaborated in –The Chapter on Directive Principles of State Policy, Fundamental Rights, and Fundamental Duties

                            Preamble's ideals are elaborated in Fundamental Rights, Directive Principles and Fundamental Duties; the Preamble reflects the Constitution's objectives. Must know

                            Full question and explanation · 3 paper(s)

                            • How many types of justice has been enshrined in the Preamble of the Constitution of India?Three

                            Preamble → 3 types of justice: social, economic and political. Must know

                            Full question and explanation · 2 paper(s)

                            • Economic Justice’ as one of the objectives of the Indian Constitution has been provided in –The Preamble and the Directive Principles of State Policy

                            Economic Justice → in the Preamble and in DPSP (e.g. Art. 38(1): a social order with social, economic and political justice).

                            Full question and explanation · 1 paper(s)

                            • The Preamble to the Constitution of India is:a part of the Constitution but has no legal effect independently of other parts

                            Preamble → part of the Constitution (Kesavananda Bharati, 1973) but not enforceable in court; it has no legal effect on its own.

                            Full question and explanation · 1 paper(s)

                            • The Preamble given in the Constitution—

                            Preamble: not enforceable in courts, important and useful, states aims of governance, aids judicial interpretation; amended only once, 1976 (42nd Amendment).

                            Full question and explanation · 1 paper(s)

                            • Which of the following is correct?Social equality is guaranteed in our Constitution

                            Social equality is guaranteed by the Constitution → Right to Equality, Arts 14-18; the Preamble also aims at it.

                            Full question and explanation · 1 paper(s)

                                  The Governance System + The Governance System

                                  79 facts · 82 questions · 7 Must know

                                  Read the key facts and each question with its answer (30 min), then cover the answers and recall (10 min). Open the chapter in the full notes for explanations.
                                  The Governance System: key facts from the book
                                  • A Government is an institution or a system made of a group of people that takes care of or manages a country or a State. Every Government has its own Constitution or a set of fundamental principles that it follows to ensure effective governance.
                                  • An autocracy is a form of Government where the supreme power or rule is in the hands of one individual or entity.
                                  • Autocracy includes an absolute monarchy, where a family or a group of families rule a country.
                                  • The post of monarch is inherited in an absolute monarchy.
                                  • Monarchy is one of the oldest forms of Government. Now, autocracy also includes dictatorship.
                                  • Dictatorship is a form of Government in which an individual possesses absolute power without any effective limitations.
                                  • Democracy is the most widely adopted system of Governance at present. In this form of Government, the final power resides with the people.
                                  • The State has four essential elements - Population, Territory, Government and Sovereignty. Sovereignty is the most important element.
                                  • India, before 1947, was not a State because though it had three other elements,
                                  • i.e. population, territory and Government; the fourth and most important one, i.e. sovereignty, was missing because of British control over India.
                                  • There are mainly two types of systems of Governance – Parliamentary and Presidential.
                                  • India follows a Parliamentary form of government which is influenced by the Parliamentary system of the United Kingdom.
                                  • In the Parliamentary system, members of the executive branch are usually taken from the Legislature and are also accountable to the legislature. The Parliamentary system of Government is also known as the Cabinet form of Government.
                                  • The government is responsible to the popular House of the legislature and remains in power till it has the support of a majority of members in that House. Thus, the Cabinet form of Government is a mechanism to ensure the collective responsibility of the Government to House of the people.
                                  • In India, the Cabinet is headed by the Head of the Government, the Prime Minister.
                                  • The Head of the State is the President.
                                  • India is a Democratic Republic where the Supreme power is vested in the people of India.
                                  • The Indian political system does not provide for a unified authority but makes a division of powers between the Union and the States.
                                  • The Indian Constitution has both Federal and Unitary features. In its Federal characteristic, it has a written Constitution, division of powers between centre and States, independent judiciary and bicameral legislature, etc.
                                  • However, it also includes unitary features like single citizenship, the appointment of Governors by the President, Declaration of emergency and the power of parliament for implementation of international agreements.
                                  • In the Presidential form of Government, the President is the head of the executive branch.
                                  • The best example of the Presidential form of Government is the Government of the USA. Granville Austin described Indian Federalism as Cooperative Federalism. K.C. Wheare describes it as Quasi – federal. Dr. B.R. Ambedkar stated that the Constitution has not been set in a tight mould of federalism, that is, it contains both federal and unitary features.

Wheare describes it as Quasi – federal. Dr. B.R. Ambedkar stated that the Constitution has not been set in a tight mould of federalism, that is, it contains both federal and unitary features.
                                  • Which one of the following best defines the term ‘State?A community of persons permanently occupying a definite territory independent of external control and possessing an organized government

                                  State (Garner) → community of people permanently occupying a definite territory, independent of external control, with an organised government the people obey.

                                  Full question and explanation · 1 paper(s)

                                  • Which one is the most prominent element of a state?Sovereignty

                                  Four elements of a State: population, territory, government, sovereignty; sovereignty is the most important (pre-1947 India lacked it).

                                  Full question and explanation · 1 paper(s)

                                  • With reference to the Sovereignty of India, which of the following statements is/are correct?1 only

                                  India is a Commonwealth member and accepts the British Crown as Commonwealth head (1947 declaration), but this extra-constitutional step does not curtail its sovereignty.

                                  Full question and explanation · 1 paper(s)

                                  • The idea of the Preamble has been borrowed in Indian Constitution from the Constitution of –U.S.A.

                                  Idea of the Preamble → from the US Constitution; its language → from the Australian Constitution.

                                  Don't confuse The idea (USA) with the language (Australia).

                                  Full question and explanation · 1 paper(s)

                                  • Constitution of India provides which type of governance system?Parliamentary

                                  Indian Constitution → Parliamentary form of government, modelled on the UK; executive draws legitimacy from and is accountable to the legislature.

                                  Full question and explanation · 1 paper(s)

                                  • In a Parliamentary system of Government –Legislature controls Executive

                                  In a Parliamentary system, the Legislature controls the Executive.

                                  Full question and explanation · 1 paper(s)

                                  • A Parliamentary System of Government is one in which:the Government is responsible to the Parliament and can be removed by it

                                  Parliamentary (Cabinet) system → Government drawn from and responsible to Parliament; stays in power only while it has majority support in the popular house.

                                  Full question and explanation · 1 paper(s)

                                  • The Parliamentary form of Government was first introduced in which country?Great Britain (UK)

                                  Parliamentary form of government first emerged in Great Britain (UK). Must know

                                  Full question and explanation · 2 paper(s)

                                  • The Indian Parliamentary System is different from the British Parliamentary System in that India has:The system of judicial review

                                  India's parliamentary system differs from Britain's by having judicial review (from US Constitution); real and nominal executive, collective responsibility, bicameralism are common to both.

                                  Full question and explanation · 1 paper(s)

                                  • We adopted parliamentary democracy based on the British model, but how does our model differ from that model?Both 1 and 2

                                  British Parliament is sovereign; Indian Parliament's law-making power is limited, and constitutionality of amendments goes to a Supreme Court Constitution Bench. Both statements true.

                                  Full question and explanation · 1 paper(s)

                                  • Which one of the following is not the feature of Indian Constitution?Presidential Government

                                  Indian Constitution features: Parliamentary government, independent judiciary, federal government; Presidential government is not a feature.

                                  Full question and explanation · 1 paper(s)

                                  • Which one of the following is incorrect about the Indian Political System?Presidential System of the Government

                                  India has Parliamentary, not Presidential, government: President is nominal head; real executive is Council of Ministers under PM; India is secular and federal.

                                  Full question and explanation · 1 paper(s)

                                  • Given below are two statements, one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other as Reason (R).Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).

                                  India is Parliamentary because the executive (Council of Ministers under PM) is collectively responsible to the legislature, mainly Lok Sabha (Art. 75(3)); A and R true, R explains A.

                                  Full question and explanation · 1 paper(s)

                                  • There is parliamentary system of Government in India because theCouncil of Ministers is responsible to the Lok Sabha

                                  India has a Parliamentary system because the Council of Ministers is responsible to the Lok Sabha; executive members come from the legislature.

                                  Full question and explanation · 1 paper(s)

                                  • The main advantage of the parliamentary form of government is thatthe executive remains responsible to the legislature

                                  Main advantage of Parliamentary government → the executive stays responsible to the legislature, giving a responsible government.

                                  Full question and explanation · 1 paper(s)

                                  • In the context of India, which of the following principles is/are implied institutionally in the Parliamentary Government?1 and 2

                                  Parliamentary government implies: Cabinet members are MPs; ministers stay while they enjoy Parliament's confidence; Cabinet is not headed by Head of State. Non-MP minister goes after six months (Art. 75(5)).

                                  Full question and explanation · 1 paper(s)

                                  • Which one of the following statements is correct regarding parliamentary form of government?None of the above/More than one of the above

                                  Parliamentary government: executive responsible to legislature, majority rule, collective responsibility, nominal and real executives, double membership, PM's leadership, dissolution of lower house.

                                  Full question and explanation · 1 paper(s)

                                  • Out of the following statements, choose the one that brings out the principle underlying the Cabinet form of Government:A mechanism of parliamentary democracy for ensuring collective responsibility of the Government to the people

                                  Cabinet form (responsible government) → mechanism of parliamentary democracy ensuring collective responsibility of the Government to the people.

                                  Full question and explanation · 1 paper(s)

                                  • In a Presidential Government, all the executive powers are vested in –President

                                  Presidential government → all executive powers vest in the President, who is both head of State and head of Government.

                                  Full question and explanation · 1 paper(s)

                                  • The cardinal features of political system in India are –1, 2 and 3

                                  Indian political system: democratic republic, parliamentary government, supreme power with the people; no unified authority, as powers are separated between Union and States. Must know

                                  Full question and explanation · 2 paper(s)

                                  • Consider the following statements:1, 2, 3 and 4

                                        National Symbols

                                        14 facts · 16 questions · 2 Must know

                                        Read the key facts and each question with its answer (30 min), then cover the answers and recall (10 min). Open the chapter in the full notes for explanations.
                                        National Symbols: key facts from the book
                                        • The National Flag (Tricolour) is rectangular in shape and consists of three colours.
                                        • The ratio of the length of the flag to its width is 3:2.
                                        • The colour of the top band is Indian saffron (Kesariya) (symbol of strength and courage), the middle band is white (symbol of peace and truth) and the bottom is Indian green (symbol offertility, growth and auspiciousness of the land).
                                        • In the centre of the white band is a navy blue wheel, which represents the Ashoka chakra. It has 24 spokes, and its design is that of the wheel, which appears on the abacus of the Sarnath lion capital of Ashoka.
                                        • It is the symbol of Justice- (Wheel of the law/Dharma Chakra).
                                        • The National flag was designed by Pingali Venkayya.
                                        • The present design of the national flag was adopted by the constituent assembly on 22 July, 1947.
                                        • The description of the importance of three colours and a wheel (chakra) in our national flag by Dr. S. Radhakrishnan is mentioned and reproduced in the Flag code of India.
                                        • The state emblem is an adaptation of the Sarnath lion capital of Ashoka.
                                        • It was adopted by the Government of India on 26 January, 1950.
                                        • The words 'Satyameva Jayate' from Mundaka Upanishad are inscribed at the bottom in the Devanagari Script.
                                        • The National Anthem of India 'Jana Gana Mana.....' was officially adopted by the constituent assembly on 24th January, 1950.
                                        • It was first sung on 27th December, 1911 at the Calcutta session of the Indian National Congress (President- Pt. Bishan Narayan Dar).
                                        • It was authored by Rabindra Nath Tagore. The Playing time of the full version is approximately 52 seconds.
                                        • The song 'Vande Mataram' was adopted as the national song by the constituent assembly on 24 January, 1950. It is taken from the novel "Anand Math" authored by Bankimchandra Chatterjee.
                                        • It was first sung at the 1896 session of the Indian National Congress (President -Rahimatullah Sayani).
                                        • The National Calendar based on the Saka era (Chaitra as its first month and Falgun as the last) was adopted on 22nd March, 1957 along with the Gregorian Calendar. Generally, the month of Chaitra begins on 22 March, but in the leap years, it begins on 21 March.
                                        • The National Flower of India is the Lotus (Nelumbo nucifera Gaertn). The National fruit is Mango (Magnifera Indica).
                                        • The National tree is the Banyan tree (Ficus benghalensis).
                                        • While the government has clearly stated in the Rajya Sabha that no notification has been issued regarding India having a National flower.
                                        • The National Animal is the magnificent Tiger (Panthera tigris).
                                        • The National Bird is the Indian Peacock (Pavo cristatus).
                                        • The National Aquatic animal is the mammal Ganges River Dolphin (Platanista gangetica).
                                        • The river Ganga was declared the national river by the government of India in the year 2008.
                                        • The Government of India declared the Independence Day (15 August), Republic Day (26 January) and the Birth Anniversary of Mahatama Gandhi (2 October) as National Days.
                                        • In which year was ‘Jana Gana Mana’ adopted as the National Anthem of India?1950

                                        'Jana Gana Mana' adopted as National Anthem by the Constituent Assembly on 24 January 1950; full rendition takes fifty-two seconds.

                                        Full question and explanation · 1 paper(s)

                                        • When the Hindi version of National Anthem Jana Gana-Mana was adopted by the Constituent Assembly of India?24 January, 1950

                                        Jana-Gana-Mana: composed in Bengali by Rabindranath Tagore; Hindi version adopted 24 January 1950; first sung 27 December 1911, Calcutta Congress session.

                                        Full question and explanation · 1 paper(s)

                                        • A complete or formal rendition of national anthem takes-52 seconds

                                        National Anthem → full rendition about 52 seconds; short version (first and last lines) 20 seconds.

                                        Full question and explanation · 1 paper(s)

                                        • The state emblem was adopted by Govt. of India on -26th January, 1950

                                        State Emblem (from Ashoka pillar, Sarnath, Varanasi) → adopted by Government of India on 26 January 1950.

                                        Full question and explanation · 1 paper(s)

                                        • When did the Constituent Assembly adopt the National Flag?22 July, 1947

                                        National Flag adopted by the Constituent Assembly on 22 July 1947, in its fourth session.

                                              States and the Union Territories

                                              50 facts · 63 questions · 12 Must know

                                              Read the key facts and each question with its answer (30 min), then cover the answers and recall (10 min). Open the chapter in the full notes for explanations.
                                              States and the Union Territories: key facts from the book
                                              • The Indian Independence Act of 1947 led to the formation of two independent and separate Dominions – India and Pakistan. The Princely States were provided three options – to join India, to join Pakistan or to remain Independent.
                                              • There were more than 560 princely States within the Indian territory, out of which most joined India, whereas three (Hyderabad, Junagadh and Kashmir) refused to join India.
                                              • Later on, Hyderabad through military Action, Junagadh through a referendum and Kashmir through the Instrument of Accession (a legal document) executed by Maharaja Hari Singh (ruler of the Jammu & Kashmir) were included in the Indian Union. The Indian Constitution that came into force in 1950 went a step further, recognising four different categories of States and territories in the first Schedule. Part A was comprised of former British India provinces, which had a governor and a Legislature. Part B was comprised of former Princely States governed by a 'raj pramukh' while Part C was a combination of Princely States and chief commissioner's provinces governed by a chief commissioner. Part D was comprised of the lone territory of the Andaman and Nicobar Islands administered by the President through a Chief Commissioner/Other authority appointed by him. It was Part C states and part D territories that would go on to form the basis for the creation of Union Territories.
                                              • As per the Article 1(1) of the Constitution, “India, that is Bharat, shall be a Union of States” rather than the Federation of States.
                                              • Article 2 provides for the admission or establishment of New States.
                                              • Article 3 provides for the power of the Parliament in the formation of New States and alteration of areas, boundaries and names of existing States.
                                              • Parliament can form new States through a simple majority.
                                              • Amendments made under Articles 2 and 3 are out of the scope of Article 368.
                                              • Presently, India comprises 28 States and 8 Union Territories. S.K. Dhar Commission 1948 recommended the reorganization of States on the basis of administrative convenience instead of a linguistic basis.
                                              • In December 1948, the JVP committee was constituted by the Congress to scrutinize the recommendations of the S.K. Dhar Commission.
                                              • This committee included Jawahar Lal Nehru, Vallabh Bhai Patel and Pattabhi Sitaramaiya.
                                              • The committee, in its report presented in April 1949, officially rejected the demand for the reorganization of the States on linguistic basis.
                                              • Although the demise of Potti Sriramulu after the 56-day-long hunger strike forced the Indian Government for the formation of Andhra Pradesh on linguistic basis in October, 1953.
                                              • Andhra Pradesh is the first State of India formed on the linguistic basis.
                                              • A States Reorganisation Commission under the Chairmanship of Fazal Ali was constituted for the formation of new States in 1953.
                                              • Two other members of this Commission were – K.M. Panikkar and H.N. Kunzru.
                                              • Some of the recommendations of this commission were implemented in the States Reorganisation Act, 1956.
                                              • Consider the following statements about Union and its Territory.Both 1 and 2

                                              India, a Union of States, is a Sovereign Socialist Secular Democratic Republic with parliamentary government; 28 States and 8 Union Territories; both statements true.

                                              Full question and explanation · 1 paper(s)

                                              Full question and explanation · 1 paper(s)

                                              • According to Article 1 of Indian Constitution, India is –The Union of States

                                              Art. 1 → India is a 'Union of States'; territory = States, Union Territories and territories acquired; names in First Schedule.

                                              Full question and explanation · 1 paper(s)

                                              • Indian Parliament has the power to create a new State under which of the following Constitutional provisions?Article 3

                                              Art. 3 → Parliament forms new States (separating or uniting territory); Art. 2 → Parliament admits or establishes new States.

                                              Full question and explanation · 1 paper(s)

                                              • The power to carve out a new State is vested in –The Parliament

                                              Power to create new States and alter boundaries, area or names → Parliament (Art. 2: admit or establish; Art. 3: form, alter). Must know

                                              Don't confuse Not the President or a States Reorganisation Commission: only Parliament, by law.

                                              Full question and explanation · 5 paper(s)

                                              • Which one of the following is not correct in the matter of formation of new States?Such law shall be deemed to be an amendment of the Constitution for the purpose of Article 368.

                                              Law forming a new State amends First and Fourth Schedules but is not a constitutional amendment under Art. 368 (Art. 4(2)); simple majority is enough.

                                              Creating a new State → simple majority in Parliament, ordinary legislative process; not an amendment under Art. 368. Must know

                                              Full question and explanation · 2 paper(s)

                                              • Assertion (A): India is not a Union.(A) is false, but (R) is true.

                                              Altering a State's name → power of Parliament (Art. 3), not State Legislature; equality before law → citizens and non-citizens; equal opportunity in public employment → citizens only.

                                              Full question and explanation · 1 paper(s)

                                              • Which among the following is not a ‘constitutional provision for the formation of new States?A State may include a Union territory.

                                              Under Art. 3 only Parliament can increase, diminish, alter boundaries or name of a State; a State cannot add territory by itself; 'State' here includes a Union Territory.

                                              Full question and explanation · 1 paper(s)

                                              • Which of the following is NOT possible by a law of Parliament under Article 3 of the Constitution?Admission of new States

                                              Art. 3 → formation of new States and alteration of their areas, boundaries, names; admission of new States is not under Art. 3.

                                              Full question and explanation · 1 paper(s)

                                              • Consider the following statement and answer using codes given below:All of the above

                                              Full question and explanation · 1 paper(s)

                                              • With reference to the federal system in India, which of the Statements is/are correct?1 only

                                              States have no right to secede; Parliament can alter them by simple majority (true). Advocacy of secession is not protected by freedom of expression (false).

                                              Full question and explanation · 1 paper(s)

                                              • How many States and UTs did the States Reorganisation Commission create in 1956?14 States and 6 UTs

                                              • How many States and Union Territories are there in India?None of the above

                                              Full question and explanation · 4 paper(s)

                                              • Which of the following is not a Union Territory?Goa

                                              Goa is a State; Andaman and Nicobar, Daman and Diu, Puducherry are UTs; First Schedule lists States and UTs (28 States, 8 UTs).

                                              • Delhi is a/an –Union territory
